よめる ように なりたい — I want to be able to read
You say what you CAN and CAN’T do with the potential form (よめる, たべられる, できる, こられる) and how you come to be able to: ～ように なる.
to be able to do; to know how (to)
to come to be able to
I’ve become able to speak a little Japanese.
I want to read the letter by myself.
To form the potential of group 1 verbs (よむ → よめる).
To form the potential of group 2 verbs (たべる → たべられる) and the irregular ones (する → できる, くる → こられる).
To use the particle が with the potential: にほんご が はなせます.
To say how you’ve progressed: ～ように なりました (I’ve become able to).
To learn your first kanji: 山, 川, 人, 日.
December, in Madrid. Mihai has received a letter from Mrs Fumiko, Mrs Suzuki’s sister. It’s written with lots of kanji. Mihai takes it to the library.
Mrs Suzuki, can you read this? It’s a letter from Mrs Fumiko.
Oh, from Fumiko? Yes, I can read it. But can’t you?
I can read hiragana and katakana. But I can’t read kanji at all.
Well, Fumiko is someone who can write an awful lot of kanji.
I want to become able to read it. I want to read Mrs Fumiko’s letter by myself.
Then shall I teach you kanji here, every Saturday?
Really? But you’re busy, aren’t you?
I can come on Saturday afternoons. And I can bring Tama too.
Tama too? Can you bring a cat to the library?
That’s a secret. Learn kanji a little at a time every day. In a year you can memorise about a hundred.
A hundred! I’ll do my best.
The first kanji is this: 山. It’s read “yama” (mountain).
Oh, the shape looks like a mountain! I can remember this one.
“sukoshi zutsu” = a little at a time
ra-re-ru: two syllables with “r” in a row; the tongue lightly taps the roof of the mouth each time, like a soft “d”.
yo-me-ru, yo-me-mas: the stress is neutral, and the final “u” of ます almost disappears.
kan-ji: the “n” is a whole syllable; don’t say “ka-nji”.
For group 1 verbs, the last syllable moves from the “u” column to the “e” column and you add る. The polite form: ～ます.
Potential forms all conjugate like group 2 verbs: よめない (can’t read), よめた (could read), よめて…
Group 2: る → られる. And する becomes a completely different verb: できる. べんきょう する → べんきょう できる.
In everyday speech, young people often say たべれる, みれる, これる (without “ra”). It’s very widespread, but in exams and in writing use the full form: たべられる.
3. The particle が with the potential
With the potential form, the object usually takes が instead of を:
It’s the same logic as with すき, わかる and ～たい: the thing you “can” do is the grammatical subject. You still often hear を in conversation; it isn’t a serious mistake.
4. ～ように なる: I’ve become able to
Potential (dictionary form) + ように なる = a gradual change: “I’ve become able to”.
I’ve become able to read kanji.
I want to become able to speak a little.
I’ve become able to eat nattō!
The first kanji: 山 (やま, mountain), 川 (かわ, river), 人 (ひと, person), 日 (ひ / にち, day, sun). They all come from pictures: a mountain with three peaks, flowing water, a person walking, a sun.

はじめて の かんじ — The first kanji
At the beginning of December, it turned cold in Madrid.
One morning, a letter from Japan arrived at Mihai’s home.
On the envelope, in beautiful handwriting, it said: “To Mr Mihai and Ms Ana”.
The sender was Mrs Fumiko in Kyoto, Mrs Suzuki’s younger sister.
Mihai was delighted and opened the envelope straight away.
But when he looked at the letter, his face fell.
It was full of kanji. Hiragana only appeared here and there.
“I can’t read it… I can’t read it at all.”
Ana looked at it with him, but she couldn’t read it either.
The only thing they understood was the name at the end, “Fumiko”.
“No. I want to read it by myself. Mrs Fumiko wrote it by hand for us.”
From that day, Mihai’s kanji study began.
On Saturday afternoons, in a little room at the library, Mrs Suzuki taught him kanji.
Tama always slept on the desk.
On the first day he learned 山, 川 and 人.
山 is shaped like a mountain, 川 like flowing water, 人 like a person walking.
“Kanji are pictures. Try thinking of them as pictures,” said Mrs Suzuki.
Mihai wrote them in his notebook countless times. He decided to learn five a day.
But kanji weren’t easy at all.
“Why does a single kanji have so many readings?!”
When Mihai asked this with a glum face, Mrs Suzuki laughed.
“Japanese children say the same thing. But they all become able to read them.”
Even at Christmas, Mihai had kanji flashcards in his pocket.
He looked at them on the metro, and while waiting for ramen at Kenji’s place.
“Mihai, your noodles are going soggy!” Kenji laughed.
“Wait. One more. When I can read this one, I’ll eat.”
By the end of January, Mihai had become able to read fifty kanji.
Ana was busy with her Spanish classes and could only study a little.
But every evening she looked at Mihai’s notebook and they studied together.
And one evening in February, Mihai opened Mrs Fumiko’s letter again.
He could read the first line: “The cold days continue. Are you well?”
And he could read the next line: “Since I became able to talk to my sister again, every day is a joy.”
Mihai’s voice trembled a little. Ana was listening beside him.
“It’s thanks to you two. Thank you from the bottom of my heart.”
There were kanji he didn’t know. But, unlike before, Mihai could look them up in the dictionary.
When he read the last line, Mihai was lost for words.
“Congratulations on your marriage. I’m coming to Madrid for the wedding in May, together with my sister.”
“Ana… Mrs Fumiko and Mrs Suzuki are both coming!”
Ana looked at the letter, then at Mihai, and smiled.
“Mihai, you read the whole thing by yourself just now.” “…Yes. I could.”
The following Saturday, Mihai showed the letter to Mrs Suzuki at the library.
Mrs Suzuki already knew, because Mrs Fumiko had phoned her.
“You know, Fumiko used lots of kanji on purpose. Because she thought that you, of all people, would surely become able to read them.”
Mihai smiled and wrote in big letters on a new page of his notebook: 山.
It was the first kanji Mihai had learned.
Tama miaowed on the desk. As if to say: “Well done, you did it”.
